To fix Codebook Check

What we found

We found no codebook or README documentation for the 1050 extracted data columns.

Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 1 codebook/README/label source and 1050 data columns across 16 files.

No codebook or README documentation was found, so no data columns could be matched to variable definitions.

Duplicated Column Names

  • Duplicated column names in novice_survey.csv. 1 column name appears more than once (worst: Rec_Session_Id×2), so 2 of the file’s 73 columns share a name with another. This usually means a survey loop/merge exported repeated blocks without numbering each iteration; the repeats cannot be told apart and can only be documented once. Consider re-exporting with per-iteration column names.

To check (4)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 13 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Code Comments

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.

Missing Files

All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 4 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Susan is a 14 year old girl whom, ever since she was seven, was involved in ballet classes. Initially she was set up to do ballet because her mom wanted her to be involved. She was kind of annoyed at first, but as time grew on, she got better and better, she grew to love ballet. One day, she had a dance competition to prepare for. She knew that she was good at what she did, and that she was going to do anything she could to be able to win that dance competition. As she began to walk towards the ballet studio, she saw a poster for a missing dog named ‘Fido’. She immediately felt bad for the dog, and would promise herself to be on the lookout for it. She continued on her way to the ballet studio and she gave it her all during the competition. There are other girls involved, and they were each clearly well-trained, and were trying their best to win the competition. After the competition ended, the judges met and they decided that Susan was in fact the winner. She was so excited that her mom and her dad decided to take her out for a special lunch at a local restaurant that Susan happened to absolutely love. At the restaurant, they each ordered a cup of tea, which was customary of them. While Susan was stirring her cup of tea, she heard a barking. She looked over and she saw the dog from the poster and she got even more excited. This was her chance to not only be given something good by winning a competition, being given the title the best of that competition; but to be able to give something good back to somebody else, who is desperately looking for their missing dog. Susan excitedly told her parents about the poster that she had seen, and they went over and they were able to capture the dog who initially was frightened, but ultimately was overjoyed when it was later reunited by Susan, with its owner who was another girl around Susan’s age. Ultimately the story had a very happy ending. and that is the end of the story. 1 , 1 2 1 a cup of tea, a missing dog, a dance competition 0.9960 NA NA NA NA NA 18 381 195 0.5118110 2002 21.16667 text1 64.70213 0.2020997 0.4535809 3 1 OM1 4 3 2 26.850000 2 1 NA 1 NA 1 2 1 5 2 1 TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE

And there was a big dance competition that day. Everyday, she would have a cup of tea at midday. And that was just her thing. This is what she would do is every day at midday, she would have a nice cup of tea. And this day being like any other day for her, with the exception of it being a dance competition day, she was going to have her cup of tea. She sat down to make her tea. While she was making the tea, as the water was boiling, there was a knock at her door. Tiffany being the 14 year old girl that she was, not at all worried or concerned that somebody would be knocking on her door on noon on a Saturday, she went to answer the door. When she answered the door, there was a young boy and he said, “miss miss, can you help me?” He was about six years old and you could see that he’d been crying, and his pants were a little ripped. And she asked him why he was crying and what, what he wanted. He said, “well, I’ve lost my dog.” And Tiffany said, “what? You have a missing dog?” He said, “yes, can you help me find it?” Tiffany decided to put aside her cup of tea and help this young boy find his missing dog. So she left her house, went out, and they started walking around looking for this missing dog. And she was kind of following the boy a little bit, because he was describing the dog, and talking about where he had last seen it. And he goes, “I think it went over this way.” So she followed him behind this old house, this nasty looking old house that she had never really noticed in the neighborhood. And as she was following him, she turned around and realized that the boy who disappeared. And then she looked up and there was a large, ugly, strange man in front of her. And he grabbed her and he dragged her into the house. And he dragged her into the basement of the house and tied her up. It turns out there never was a missing dog, and that he was just a creepy man. And he used his grandson to lure young girls into his basement. She was tied up in that basement for several hours. And he never came to check on her or anything, but eventually she did wind up getting herself loose. So although there was no missing dog, she never did get her cup of tea, and she did miss her dance competition, she was able to escape the house and nothing bad happened to her. And that’s the end of the story. 1 , 10 4 2 a cup of tea, a missing dog, a dance competition 0.4233 NA NA NA NA NA 34 520 236 0.4538462 2610 15.29412 text2 84.19122 0.1250000 0.3781676 3 1 198 2 1 1 8.981750 NA 1 I majored in British Literature at xxx university native 1 35 A creative story is a narrative that explores imaginative concepts, characters, and settings, often incorporating original or inventive elements to evoke emotions, provoke thought, or entertain. There were some blacked out channels which are paid content only. Then she finally found the history channel and there was a long, long story about a missing dog. The dog had belonged to an emperor of Russia, and it was his favorite dog. The hunt to find this dog was so massive and dragged out, the woman could not believe the story she was hearing. Then that program finished, but she didn’t get to see the ending of it because she fell asleep, being so tired. She watched this show and thought, it was really sad, obnoxious, how crazy the parents were, and how much the girls were stressed out about being in this pageant. She didn’t really think anybody was having fun, the parents or the little girls. After a while, she got bored again and picked up her smartphone and started actually trying to find directions around the seat to get to where she wanted to go. She was able to finally download Google maps and learned how to use it. That way, she didn’t really get lost anymore. She had a great time in the city. Assessing the creativity of a story involves considering several key criteria:
Originality: The extent to which the story presents fresh ideas, concepts, characters, or settings that are not derivative of existing works. A truly creative story introduces elements that feel new and innovative.
Imagination: The vividness and richness of the author’s imagination as demonstrated through the world-building, character development, and plot intricacies. It is so wonderful for a pet in New York City to have that unconditional love and sense of purpose. And adopting a dog, this couple, Anthony, and his wife, Terry, they felt they were doing a good deed by adopting a dog from a shelter, a kill shelter and giving it the best life they could. They opted not to have children. And they thought that having an adopted dog would be the best way to share love with another being. So they hired a dog walking service that would come in twice a day, since they both worked nine to five. Anthony was at work one day and he got a call from the dog walker. She explained that she had been walking their dog through Central Park and he’d gotten off the leash. Their dog’s name was Liam. Liam had escaped. And so quickly Anthony called his wife, Terry, and he said, “oh my goodness, we have a missing dog. Our dog is missing.” He could hardly speak. His wife, Terry quickly punched out of work and began to retrace the steps of the dog walker. And she realized that the dog walker had stopped first for a cup of tea, and that she had latched the dog, his leash, to a fire hydrant. And that’s how he became missing. He didn’t just get off the leash. She didn’t escape. She was distracted getting a cup of tea, and she takes her eyes off the thing that meant the most to them. Terry then called the dog walker and she said, “I’m so upset. I’m trying to find my pet. I’m frantic. It means the world to me and my husband, Anthony. Please, can you help us?” The dog walker said, “I feel extraordinarily guilty. I really do. I’m so sorry right now though. I can’t speak. I’m at a dance competition for my youngest daughter. I’m sure you’ll understand that. I need to really be concentrating on my daughter and the dance competition. And when I’m finished, I’ll return your call.” Terry hung up the phone and she was incensed. For Anthony and Terry, their dog was just as much a family member. They felt the same way about their dog as the dog walker felt about her daughter. Eventually Anthony and Terry put up signs about their missing dog, Liam, and they hardly slept or ate. And about two days later, they walked outside their apartment door. And their missing dog, Liam was sitting outside, waiting for them. He knew where he lived and he was looking for his family. In the end it was a happy ending. So that’s the end of the story. 1 , 12 2 3 a cup of tea, a missing dog, a dance competition 0.9085 NA NA NA NA NA 41 493 247 0.5010142 2486 12.02439 text4 84.14690 0.1480730 0.4411765 3 1 OM1 4 3 2 26.850000 2 1 NA 1 NA 1 1 3 5 2 1 TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE

2/14/24 12:10 2/14/24 13:57 0 100 6427 1 2/14/24 13:57 R_7chhMwFSORlRcqY anonymous EN PIC 6 NA NA NA NA 3 4 2 3 3 4 5 2 5 5 5 5 3 4 5 3 4 3 4 4 4 5 5 2 4 3 3 3 3 4 3 2 4 2 3 3 2 4 2 2 4 3 4 4 5 5 4 3 4 5 4 4 4 5 4 5 5 4 5 5 4 2 5 3 3 4 4 5 2 5 4 5 2 4 4 4 5 5 3 5 3 2 3 3 4 3 3 3 1 2 I think all of these dimensions are relevant to assess story creativity. However, I found myself not being entirely sure how to evaluate ““novelty”” as the study progressed. Was I supposed to rate the story as novel in general, or novel given the clear common factors across many of these stories? I also think that, when I consider a story creative, its novelty isn’t necessarily the most strongly weighted component…depending on what the novelty consists of, I suppose. So, for example novel settings vs places vs characters vs plot points may change how creative I perceive a story more or less. I think the relationship between expected plot points and unexpected plot points / details probably has the strongest bearing on my understanding of creativity. There can be a simple but creative story as well; complex details tended, to me, to suggest a more imaginative story because they fleshed out character/setting/plot more. I found these things seemed to correlate and sometimes I had trouble distinguishing the two when I was rating because complexity felt so causal to imagination. Cohesion seemed to relate more to my satisfaction as a reader and my ability to see a strong (or weak) arc to the narrative. I think many creative stories don’t have to be cohesive; I do think that many cohesive stories aren’t necessarily creative. I could see some correlation here, but it felt like there was a very different relationship between cohesion and creativity in these stories than in say imagination / complexity and creativity. character (whether that is human or not), plot points/development, details, and audience expectations all seemed really critical to me during the study and in my general sense of creative storytelling. A story about a princess in a tower with a dragon isn’t really creative necessarily, but Shrek really was because of how it played with audience expectations, imo. Some of the more creative stories drew on common elements of the study but interpreted them in neat ways, with more fleshed out identities/motivations for characters and more interesting changes in use of plot points/details.

It typically involves original characters, settings, and plots, often exploring themes, emotions, and perspectives in inventive ways. A creative story often breaks away from conventional norms, offering fresh insights, unexpected twists, and stimulating imagery. It can encompass various genres, including fantasy, science fiction, mystery, romance, horror, and more. Ultimately, a creative story aims to captivate and resonate with its audience through its creativity, originality, and artistry. Assessing the creativity of a story involves considering several key criteria:
Originality: The extent to which the story presents fresh ideas, concepts, characters, or settings that are not derivative of existing works. A truly creative story introduces elements that feel new and innovative.
Imagination: The vividness and richness of the author’s imagination as demonstrated through the world-building, character development, and plot intricacies. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 1050 columns across 16 data files.

Issues Identified

62 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

43 distinct respondents were flagged for straightlining: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is one row per person, and the Longest run column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, 43 were flagged only by short-scale straightlining (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.

These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

What this does not cover. Only 1 of 16 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Reproducibility Check

We ran the paper’s 4 R scripts and 4 Python scripts in the order they depend on each other, each in an isolated container, for at most 5 minutes per script. 6 identical copies of these scripts, which other links in the paper lead to, were not run again.

3 of 8 scripts ran to the end: 1 stopped with an error, 1 could not run on our server, 3 needed the internet.

Script Result What happened
analysis + figures v6.Rmd Ran to the end
gpt2_surprisal_entropy.ipynb Stopped It needs the internet, which is off while we run code.
analysis + figures.Rmd Stopped with an error Error in eval(predvars, data, env) : object ‘PC1’ not found
empath lexicon.ipynb Could not run on our server It needs the Python package empath, which we could not install. This is not an error in the script.
demographics.Rmd Ran to the end
longformer raw embeddings + metrics.ipynb Stopped It needs the internet, which is off while we run code.
prepare dataset.Rmd Ran to the end
sentiment analysis.ipynb Stopped It needs the internet, which is off while we run code.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A package could not be installed.

  • empath lexicon.ipynb needs empath.

empath could not be installed with the current version of R, probably because it is old. Record the versions you used (in R, renv::init() writes them to a renv.lock file) and your R version. To be sure the code keeps running, provide a Docker image: a frozen copy of the whole computer setup the code needs, which you can build from rocker/r-ver at your R version.

A script uses something it does not create or load itself.

  • analysis + figures.Rmd: PC1

Usually the object was still in your R session from earlier work, or another script made it.

  1. Restart R (in RStudio: Session > Restart R).
  2. Run each script from top to bottom, and fix what is missing.
  3. If a script needs results of another, save them to a file in the first script and read them in the second.
  4. Load every package with library() at the top.

A script downloads data while it runs.

  • gpt2_surprisal_entropy.ipynb
  • longformer raw embeddings + metrics.ipynb
  • sentiment analysis.ipynb

Online files can move, change or disappear. Save the downloaded files, add them to the deposit, and let the script read the saved copies.

Comparison with the paper

Of the 64 statistical tests reported in the paper, 51 were found in the output of the code.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 4 R code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 analysis + figures v6.Rmd — numeric
2 analysis + figures.Rmd — none
3 demographics.Rmd — none
4 prepare dataset.Rmd — none

File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 4 scripts: 3 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

demographics.Rmd ran_ok 2.1
prepare dataset.Rmd ran_ok 24.3

Undefined-variable errors

1 script failed on an undefined variable or function (object '...' not found / could not find function "..."). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper’s own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

> predictors <- c("surprisal_mean_original",

>                 
>                 'allwordpair_longformer_cos_mean',
>                 'allwordpair_longformer_cos_sd',
>                 'allsentpair_longformer_cos_mean',
>                 'allsentpair_longformer_cos_sd',

>                 'firstlast_longformer_cos',
>                 
>                 'compound_abs',
>                 'empath_n_percent',
>                 'prompt_amount',
>                 'lexical_diversity_metric'
>                 )
> results <- data.frame()
> for (y in outcomes) {
>   for (x in predictors) {
>     
>     # create the formula
>     fmla <- as.formula(paste0(y, " ~ 1 + word_n + sent_n + MLU + ", x, " + (1|story_index) + (1|raterid)"))
>     
>     # fit the model
>     model <- try(lmer(fmla, data = df_scaled), silent = TRUE)
>     
>     # check if model ran successfully
>     if (inherits(model, "try-error")) next
>     
>     coef_summary <- summary(model)$coefficients
>     
>     # initialize
>     pval <- NA
>     estimate <- NA
>     se <- NA
>     
>     # check if predictor is in the model result
>     if (x %in% rownames(coef_summary)) {
>       estimate <- coef_summary[x, "Estimate"]
>       se       <- coef_summary[x, "Std. Error"]
>       pval     <- coef_summary[x, "Pr(>|t|)"]
>       }
>     
>     # save result
>     results <- rbind(results, data.frame(outcome   = y,
>                                          predictor = x,
>                                          coef      = estimate,
>                                          se        = se,
>                                          pval      = pval
>                                          ))
>   }
>   }
> results$significant <- ifelse(results$pval < 0.05, "Significant", "Not significant")
> results$pval_adj_bh <- p.adjust(results$pval, method = "BH")
> results$significant_bh <- ifelse(results$pval_adj_bh < 0.05, "Significant", "Not significant")
> results <- results %>%

463                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     Dimension. The dimension of the characters and the world is vital in creative story telling. 
464                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 I think the ultimate theme or idea is important in a story. I think that comes out of all the elements and how they fit together at the end. If there's not an idea, then there's no point to the story. With that also, I think a good story has pacing and builds to a climax. 
465                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  
466                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  
467                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     I wish I could have heard them speaking their stories.  The mood the speakers were trying to covey, and their attitudes towards their own stories would have been a little more clear.  The clarity would have helped me past the language, grammar, and spelling issues.    
468                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               another is "creative intelligence".
469                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            I would add something to recognize quality of detail. 
470                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  
471                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  
472                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Not everything creative is good. It should be logical and believable to be a good story.

504  character (whether that is human or not), plot points/development, details, and audience expectations all seemed really critical to me during the study and in my general sense of creative storytelling. A story about a princess in a tower with a dragon isn't really creative necessarily, but Shrek really was because of how it played with audience expectations, imo. Some of the more creative stories drew on common elements of the study but interpreted them in neat ways, with more fleshed out identities/motivations for characters and more interesting changes in use of plot points/details. 
505                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              All the nuances one does not get from reading; vocal and facial inflections, body movements are all important. Sometimes the way someone tells the story is more entertaining than the story itself.

764                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     Characterization, having a climax (a number of the stories didn't) having an interesting denouement (many stories didn't). 768                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Storytelling is just like cooking. There are a lot of ingredients and depending on the context and the content the story will be balanced out well. It depends how you implement the ingredients your talent level and experience.

858                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     Dimension. The dimension of the characters and the world is vital in creative story telling. 
859                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 I think the ultimate theme or idea is important in a story. I think that comes out of all the elements and how they fit together at the end. If there's not an idea, then there's no point to the story. With that also, I think a good story has pacing and builds to a climax. 
860                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  
861                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  
862                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     I wish I could have heard them speaking their stories.  The mood the speakers were trying to covey, and their attitudes towards their own stories would have been a little more clear.  The clarity would have helped me past the language, grammar, and spelling issues.    
863                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               another is "creative intelligence".
864                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            I would add something to recognize quality of detail.

866                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  
867                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Not everything creative is good. It should be logical and believable to be a good story.

964  character (whether that is human or not), plot points/development, details, and audience expectations all seemed really critical to me during the study and in my general sense of creative storytelling. A story about a princess in a tower with a dragon isn't really creative necessarily, but Shrek really was because of how it played with audience expectations, imo. Some of the more creative stories drew on common elements of the study but interpreted them in neat ways, with more fleshed out identities/motivations for characters and more interesting changes in use of plot points/details. 
965                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              All the nuances one does not get from reading; vocal and facial inflections, body movements are all important. Sometimes the way someone tells the story is more entertaining than the story itself.

Duplicate files across repo mirrors

2 files are byte-identical to another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component that mirrors the same materials). They were only run once, from its first occurrence, to avoid wasted duplicate execution: demographics.Rmd at https://osf.io/download/687ec83c1c0056d81b0eb00d/?view_only=7c75e8804ebc40c78e19cfb4c282eb5b (same as demographics.Rmd at https://osf.io/download/699f51f68073905c22e2c453/?view_only=7c75e8804ebc40c78e19cfb4c282eb5b); prepare dataset.Rmd at https://osf.io/download/687ec85c1c0056d81b0eb011/?view_only=7c75e8804ebc40c78e19cfb4c282eb5b (same as prepare dataset.Rmd at https://osf.io/download/699f5257ded5f4c9b3e2c7d5/?view_only=7c75e8804ebc40c78e19cfb4c282eb5b).

Python code

This module also assesses whether the paper’s Python code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 4 Python code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first) and numeric filename prefixes. Python has no source()-equivalent import-based ordering signal (an import loads a module, not the paper’s own analysis flow), so that basis never applies here.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 gpt2_surprisal_entropy.ipynb — numeric
2 empath lexicon.ipynb — none
3 longformer raw embeddings + metrics.ipynb — none
4 sentiment analysis.ipynb — none

File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.

Execution

The Python code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 4 scripts: 0 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 1 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a requirements.txt). 3 scripts need the internet, which is off during the run: gpt2_surprisal_entropy.ipynb, longformer raw embeddings + metrics.ipynb, sentiment analysis.ipynb. Keeping what they download in the deposit solves this.

File Outcome Detail Time (s)
gpt2_surprisal_entropy.ipynb needs_internet 29.4
empath lexicon.ipynb dependency_unavailable dependency_unavailable 3.2
longformer raw embeddings + metrics.ipynb needs_internet 35.3
sentiment analysis.ipynb needs_internet FileNotFoundError 2.2

Dependency-unavailable errors

1 script could not run because its own dependency is unavailable — the package failed to pip install. This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so it does not force the traffic light red.

Reported vs. reproduced

64 statistical tests reported in the manuscript text were checked against the extracted analysis output: 51 matched (51 fully, 0 partially) — 79.7% found.

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The “Plausible” column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output’s own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.

Self-reproducible output (JASP / jamovi / SPSS Viewer / Jupyter notebook)

6 JASP/jamovi/SPSS-Viewer/notebook files bundle the analyses and their saved results together, so the reported statistics are recoverable from the files itself, with nothing re-run. We extracted 18 result tables (682 individual statistics), typed with the STATO ontology, and export them as a statistical-output JSON document (in the logs) and as queryable rows.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

All participants were fluent or native adult English speakers, located in the United States, with normal or corrected-to-normal hearing and vision, and access to a computer in a quiet environment.

All participants gave informed consent before starting the study.

In total, we originally recruited 100 storytellers via Prolific (https://prolific.com) to generate 6 stories each.

We recruited 316 novice raters through Prolific (age: M = 36.32, SD = 11.73, range = 18-84; gender: 191 M, 107 F, 6 unspecified; ethnicity: 197 White/Caucasian, 35 Asian, 24 Black/African American, 17 Hispanic/Latino, 1 American Indian/Alaska Native, 30 other; language: native = 294, fluent = 10; 12 excluded due to data quality issues).

In contrast, a multi-session design was less suitable for novice raters, who were recruited online to maintain a diverse and heterogeneous participant pool.

Multi-session online studies are associated with higher attrition rates (Rodd, 2024), and based on our lab’s prior experience it would have been very difficult to find online participants through Prolific to complete all sessions.

Likewise, some storytellers (even within the general population sampled in our Prolific pool) may be consistently more creative than others, and follow-up work could search for common narrative strategies or structural patterns that distinguish or cluster these storytellers based on their baseline or default level of creativity.

Ethics approval statement:

This study was approved by the Research Subjects Review Board at the University of Rochester (STUDY00005470) under the OHSP and UR policies, and in accordance with

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

We checked 84 references with DOIs. No citations to articles in the RetractionWatch database were found.
