We checked 84 references with DOIs. No citations to articles in the FLoRA database were found.

How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited (currently, a warning is provided regardless of whether the replication/reproduction study is already cited).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Full text

Abstract

The raw and processed datasets, scripts for data preprocessing, wrangling, analysis, and figures (R and Python) are available at OSF: https://osf.io/qzsy3/?view_only=7c75e8804ebc40c78e19cfb4c282eb5b.

This study has been submitted as an abstract and presented as talks and posters at several conferences and workshops.

Introduction

The perception of creative works is inherently subjective and varies widely across the human population. The same contemporary painting or novel might be considered a deeply moving masterpiece to some but unappealing or mundane to others. How do different people arrive at these diverse judgments? Are there systematic patterns underlying these divergent opinions? These questions remain poorly understood but are worth studying, since creative works-much like political beliefs and other potentially polarizing subjects-offer a valuable window into the complexity of human judgment and perception.

To rigorously study human aesthetic judgment, as well as its relation to other cognitive abilities (e.g., visual perception), and its practical applications in education, product design, and marketing (Serban et al., 2023; Sarkar & Chakrabarti, 2011), requires developing valid and reliable methods of assessment. The Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT, Amabile, 1982) has been particularly influential for this purpose, especially in the domain of creativity. In this method, experts from a specific field rate creative works along one or more dimensions (e.g., creativity, novelty, imagination) using their own subjective definitions. This approach relies on the "wisdom of experts"; that is, the general consensus among experts, regardless of their underlying reasoning, is treated as ground truth. However, reducing a multitude of ratings to a concise score summarizing experts' opinion overlooks the vast variability in human perception.

Thus, rather than relying on expert consensus to represent the "ideal" of human creative perception, a contrasting line of research has explored individual differences in aesthetic judgments (Jacobsen & Höfel, 2002; Street et al., 2016; Celikors & Field, 2025) shaped by personal, social, and educational factors. For instance, personality influences the leniency of creativity ratings (Tan et al., 2015), and social identity biases raters to perceive ideas generated by members from the same social group as more creative (Adarves-Yorno et al., 2008).

Academics from different disciplines (e.g., natural sciences vs. humanities) define the originality of scholarship in distinct ways (Guetzkow et al., 2004). Additionally, the weighting of different dimensions (e.g., novelty vs. appropriateness) in assessments of overall quality of creative products differs across cultures (Paletz & Peng, 2008).

One major source of variability in how people perceive, interpret, and evaluate complex stimuli is expertise. Cognitive scientists have conceptualized expertise from several perspectives, including the accumulation of domain-specific knowledge (through extensive training and practice) that refines perceptual sensitivity and pattern recognition, and the flexible application of knowledge to novel and complex situations (Farrington-Darby & Wilson, 2006). Domain expertise has been shown to influence ratings of the originality of visual art (Celikors & Field, 2025), poetry (Kaufman et al., 2008; Chaudhuri et al., 2024a; 2024b), and mathematical equations (Hayn-Leichsenring et al., 2022). Here, we focus on improvised oral storytelling, a form of creative expression that is more universal and accessible than these other art forms.

Stories are ubiquitous in everyday life, in the novels, news articles, and videos we consume, and in conversations we exchange with our friends. Thus, even without formal training, most people have extensive experience with storytelling, through which they may have generated implicit interpretive frameworks that inform their subjective evaluation of stories. Therefore, this medium provides a valuable opportunity to test how formal expertise differs from everyday experience, in contrast to prior work on poetry or mathematical equations, with which most people may have very limited experience.

Research investigating mechanisms of creativity perception of improvised oral stories is exceedingly rare, but a few studies have addressed the influence of expertise on creativity assessment of written short stories, finding that average creativity ratings differ relatively little between experts and novices (Kaufman et al., 2009) and that experts' and novices' ratings are strongly correlated (Taylor et al., 2021). However, it should be noted that the latter of these used "creativity researchers" as experts (instead of storytellers or writers), who also likely differed significantly in age from the undergraduate "novices", and also included only three raters per group. Furthermore, prior work has not fully taken advantage of the rich, dynamic linguistic structure of stories, which may offer deeper insights into how training in storytelling or creative writing may confer heightened or shifted sensitivity to certain structural dimensions more than others, even when overall ratings appear to be similar on the surface.

To answer this question, we measured linguistic features of human-generated stories from four diverse categories: semantic similarity, lexical predictability, lexical composition, and language productivity. These categories capture distinct aspects of linguistic information that have been investigated across diverse paradigms in story and text processing (elaborated below; e.g., Johnson et al., 2022; Laurino Dos Santos & Berger, 2022; Willems et al., 2016; Min & Park, 2019). However, previous studies have typically focused on a limited subset of linguistic features, often examining them in isolation or within specific theoretical frameworks. Here, we adopt a more integrative approach by examining multiple categories of linguistic elements, which allows us to assess their relative and complementary contributions to narrative evaluation.

The semantic similarity category is based on a comparison between embeddings, or vectorized multidimensional representations that reflect semantic relatedness between words (e.g., "ball" and "soccer" have higher similarity than "ball" and "cake"). Metrics derived from this concept have emerged as prominent predictors of creativity across tasks (AUT, word association; Heinen & Johnson et al., 2018; Beaty & Johnson, 2021; short stories; Johnson et al., 2022), based on the principle that creative thinking involves connecting distantly related concepts (Mednick, 1962; Beaty & Kenett, 2023). Semantic similarity based on context-dependent word embeddings has been shown to reliably predict human creativity ratings of short stories (lower average semantic similarity across all words predicts higher creativity; Johnson et al., 2022). Here, we build on this line of work by using Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020), a transformer model that generates contextualized embeddings (i.e., dynamic representations that integrate prior semantic context) across much longer passages than previous models (e.g., BERT; Devlin et al., 2019). We included well-established measures of word-and sentence-level semantic similarity across levels of granularity and temporal scope (e.g., average similarity across all word or sentence pairs, or across all adjacent sentence pairs; Johnson et al., 2022; Reilly et al., 2023; Toubia et al., 2021 , Skalicky et al., 2017) as well as a novel first-to-last sentence similarity measure that captures the global accumulation of semantic information across an entire story.

Next, we measured lexical predictability (surprisal and entropy), drawing on surprisal theory in sentence processing, which links comprehension difficulty under cognitive constraints to the probability of linguistic input given prior context (Hale, 2001; Levy, 2008). These measures have been shown to predict behavioral indices of language processing (e.g., reading time slowdowns : Smith & Levy, 2013; Lowder et al., 2018; Aurnhammer & Frank, 2019), as well as neural responses in ERP and fMRI studies (Frank et al., 2015; Willems et al., 2016).

Words that have high surprisal in a particular context are less predictable in that context and tend to be more difficult to process. Entropy captures the overall uncertainty associated with predicting the next token, and high entropy positions have many other similarly likely alternatives following previous text. The dual-metric approach to information-theoretic measures provides complementary insights: surprisal measures token-specific predictability, while entropy captures overall model uncertainty at each prediction point.

Our third category, lexical composition, also operates at the word level but focuses more directly on the semantic and content-related properties of language than on its abstract statistical predictability. Specifically, it includes the number of lexical categories (reflecting lexical diversity) contained in a story, the sentiment (emotionality) of words, and the number of story elements provided in the prompt (reflecting improvisational constraints). Lexical diversity has been found to predict creativity ratings of stories (Kandemirci et al., 2025) and it has been suggested that more constraints might generate more creativity (Tromp & Baer, 2022). However, these features have not been looked at together, and their relationship with other story dimensions and expertise effect has not been examined. Finally, we included measures of language productivity (e.g., word count, readability), as coarse indicators of baseline verbal fluency. Several studies have found word count to be a robust predictor of narrative creativity (Taylor et al., 2021; Johnson et al., 2022; Forthmann et al., 2018; Kandemirci et al., 2025).

Consistent with previous work (Johnson et al., 2022), we used them primarily as control variables to account for general differences in verbal output when evaluating metrics from the other three categories. This would allow us to assess whether the other linguistic features explained variation in story evaluations beyond what could be attributed to differences in the sheer quantity of language produced. The present study targets two questions regarding human evaluation of improvised spoken stories. First, we asked how expertise in storytelling and creative writing shapes ratings of different story dimensions: creativity, imagination, novelty, complexity, and cohesiveness. To capture multiple aspects of narratives while keeping the rating task manageable, we selected these dimensions based on prior empirical and theoretical work, which suggested that they capture complementary and distinct aspects of narrative evaluation (e.g., Hennessey & Amabile, 1988; Amabile, 1982; Runco & Jaeger, 2012; Graesser et al., 2011). Creativity, novelty, imagination, and complexity have been examined in prior work on creative evaluation (Hennessey & Amabile, 1988; Amabile, 1982). Cohesiveness broadly covers other rubric items included in these same studies (e.g., logic and organization), and it has been investigated more directly in research on discourse coherence and comprehension (e.g., Foltz et al., 1998; Graesser et al., 2011; McNamara et al., 2010; Crossley, 2020). We predicted that across both groups, these ratings would collapse into two main components (roughly, creativity and cohesiveness) (Patel et al., 2025). However, we also predicted that experts' training and extended practice might fine-tune their conceptualization of different dimensions (e.g., creativity vs. novelty), causing them to perceive them as more nuanced and independent from each other.

Second, we asked how expertise impacts the influence of four diverse categories of linguistic features (described above) on these ratings. Across both groups, we expect lower semantic similarity (between words or between sentences) to predict higher creativity (as in Johnson et al., 2022), but lower cohesiveness (Foltz et al., 1998). Similarly, we expect that stories with higher surprisal (and potentially, higher entropy) will be rated as more creative or novel (Filipowicz, 2006), but less cohesive, due to the added processing difficulty (Lowder et al., 2018). In terms of lexical composition, prior work has found links between the intensity of sentiment of stories and creativity ratings (Hoffmann et al., 2024), but other linguistic features in this category have not been well-studied. Here, we predict that more creative stories may have greater lexical diversity, more lexical categories, and more intense sentiment, and it is a particularly interesting open question how improvisational constraints (i.e., the number of story elements) may impact creativity vs. cohesiveness (Tromp & Baer, 2022). Finally, we tested language productivity metrics primarily as control variables so that we can isolate the meaningful effects of the other three categories. We expect story length to predict creativity ratings, a well-documented but theoretically less interesting relationship (Taylor et al., 2021; Johnson et al., 2022; Forthmann et al., 2018; Kandemirci et al., 2025). We also expect readability to be more related to cohesiveness, given its relevance to the ease of narrative processing and comprehension.

Methods

Participants

All participants were fluent or native adult English speakers, located in the United States, with normal or corrected-to-normal hearing and vision, and access to a computer in a quiet environment. This study was approved by the Research Subjects Review Board at the University of Rochester (STUDY00005470) under the OHSP and UR policies, and in accordance with

Federal regulation 45 CFR 46 under the University's Federal-wide Assurance (FWA00009386).

All participants gave informed consent before starting the study.

Storytellers

For storytellers, a working microphone was required. In total, we originally recruited 100 storytellers via Prolific (https://prolific.com) to generate 6 stories each. We plan to ultimately use this full corpus of stories to test multiple research questions, but due to financial and time constraints, for the purposes of the current study, we randomly selected 18 storytellers from the original 100, whose 6 stories each (a total of 108) were rated by experts and novices in this study (storyteller age: M = 43.67, SD = 13.97, range = 24-76; gender: 6 M, 12 F; ethnicity: 15 White/Caucasian, 1 Hispanic/Latino, 2 other; language: native = 17, fluent = 1).

Raters

We recruited 316 novice raters through Prolific (age: M = 36.32, SD = 11.73, range = 18-84; gender: 191 M, 107 F, 6 unspecified; ethnicity: 197 White/Caucasian, 35 Asian, 24 Black/African American, 17 Hispanic/Latino, 1 American Indian/Alaska Native, 30 other; language: native = 294, fluent = 10; 12 excluded due to data quality issues). We also recruited 15 expert raters through the University of Rochester's English Department and Writing Center, and from online interest groups and listservs focused on creative writing and storytelling (age: M = 32.13, SD = 17.33, range = 21-70; gender: 4 M, 3 F, 8 unspecified; ethnicity: 8 White/Caucasian, 4 Asian, 1 Black/African American, 2 other; language: 10 native, 5 fluent).

These participants self-identified as having expertise in creative writing and storytelling, with experiences in publishing poetry, performing live storytelling, and being English professors.

Expertise research has traditionally faced two related methodological challenges due to the difficulty of recruiting experts. First, expert samples are often small, which can reduce statistical power and decrease precision in parameter estimates (e.g., McAbee, 2018; Moreau, 2019). Second, expert and novice groups are often substantially imbalanced in size (e.g., Kaufman et al., 2008 Kaufman et al., , 2009: 10 experts vs. 106 novices; Phonethibsavads et al., 2023: 3 experts vs. 19 novices; Hu et al., 2023: 3 experts vs. 21 novices). Here, we made our best effort to recruit a relatively large sample of experts (i.e., larger than most relevant previous work) and match them with comparable numbers of novice raters: each story was rated by 15 experts and 10-31 novices (M = 16.89, SD = 4.06). Furthermore, our mixed-effects regression analyses modeled ratings at the story and rater level, allowing us to account for the different numbers of raters contributing to each story while directly testing the effects of expertise.

Procedures and Materials

Storytelling Task

Each storyteller completed a story generation task through the online platform Labvanced (https://www.labvanced.com/) where they improvised six novel fictional stories (each three minutes long) based on six different prompts (story word count M = 405.48, SD = 77.07; descriptive data by prompt in Table S4). Each prompt contained one to three random elements.

Example prompts included: "a pet snake," "a locked box and a love song," and "an abandoned house and a birthday card." They were given the same sentence with which to start and end each story.

Story Rating Task

Human raters scored several dimensions for 108 stories, told by 18 storytellers, each of whom created one story for each of the six prompts. Raters were given story transcripts rather than raw audio recordings (see Data Preprocessing) to eliminate effects of speech acoustics. Both expert and novice raters were given the same instructions for story evaluation. They were informed that the stories were transcripts of spoken narratives improvised in response to a given prompt, without knowing the specific prompt content or the number of elements in each prompt.

We applied the Consensual Assessment Technique (Amabile, 1982) and instructed participants to use their own definitions and subjective judgment to rate each story across five narrative dimensions, informed by previous work on creative assessment and narrative evaluation: creativity, imagination, novelty, complexity, and cohesiveness (e.g., creativity: How creative is the story?) (e.g., Amabile, 1982; Hennessey & Amabile, 1988; Runco & Jaeger, 2012; Patel et al., 2025). No examples or practice phases were provided to avoid influencing raters' judgments, consistent with prior studies (e.g., Amabile, 1982; Kaufman et al., 2007; Kaufman et al., 2008).

Ratings were made on a scale from 1 (low) to 5 (high), and both stories and rating dimensions were presented in randomized order. Raters were instructed to use the full rating scale and flip between questions and stories to revise their ratings as needed, and complete the survey in one setting in a quiet environment.

Because each story was relatively long and the study included a large number of stories, a multi-session design was necessary for expert raters to evaluate a subset of stories in each session to minimize fatigue and ensure data quality. Expert raters each completed six sessions of story evaluations on Qualtrics (https://www.qualtrics.com/). In each session, they rated 18 stories, which were based on six different prompts. Each prompt had three stories randomly drawn from different storytellers. Sessions were presented in a randomized order for each rater, and each story received ratings from 15 different expert raters.

In contrast, a multi-session design was less suitable for novice raters, who were recruited online to maintain a diverse and heterogeneous participant pool. Multi-session online studies are associated with higher attrition rates (Rodd, 2024), and based on our lab's prior experience it would have been very difficult to find online participants through Prolific to complete all sessions. Therefore, we used a modified rating procedure for novices. Novice raters completed a single session on Labvanced where they rated six randomly selected stories from the full set of 108. These stories were chosen from different speakers and prompts to ensure diversity. The stories were presented in a randomized order, and each story received ratings from between 10 and 31 novice raters (M = 16.89, SD = 4.06).

Importantly, we conducted rigorous control analyses and found no evidence that the differences in session structure between experts and novices confounded the findings of the study (Table S8).

Story Transcript Preprocessing

Story recordings were transcribed in Descript (https://www.descript.com/), an automated transcription software. These transcripts were then manually cleaned by research assistants to correct spelling and punctuation errors, and eliminate irrelevant or disfluent segments (e.g., false starts like "Tom [wrong name] is going to… Mary [correct name] is going to…" or self-corrections such as "oh sorry I'll start this sentence again"). Filler words (e.g., um, uh) were also removed from texts. Descript's automated transcription was generally accurate (>90%), but additional cues like falling intonation and pauses greater than two seconds were used to determine sentence boundaries in run-on sentences. The goal of using cleaned transcripts, rather than audio recordings or the raw transcripts, was to isolate the literal narrative content and minimize the influence of acoustic features and unrelated meta-commentaries on raters' judgments. Cleaned transcripts helped raters focus on core story elements like character development and narrative structure while generally maintaining the style of spoken language.

Feature Generation

We derived four categories of linguistic and structural features from the cleaned story transcripts: semantic similarity, lexical predictability, lexical composition, and language productivity. Semantic Similarity. Our first set of metrics was based on similarity between semantic embeddings, or vectorized multidimensional representations of the distributional properties of a given token (Turney & Pantel, 2010), to capture the relatedness between words and between sentences. Specifically, we generated contextualized word embeddings from the final layer of a transformer model, Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020), which can take relatively long documents (e.g., stories) as input, compared to similar contextual models. Using these embeddings, we computed metrics to quantify word-level similarity (mean and standard deviation across all word pairs). At the sentence-level, we tracked individual word tokens within each sentence and excluded special model tokens (e.g., <s>, </s>, <pad>). We then averaged token embeddings within each sentence to generate representative sentence-level embedding vectors (Arora et al., 2017; White et al., 2015), which were used to compute sentence-level similarity metrics (between the first and the last sentence; mean and standard deviation across all sentence pairs and across all adjacent sentence pairs); see Figure 3A for computational process. Although storytellers were instructed to start and end a story with highly similar phrasings, the embeddings for those sentences (which incorporate context) represent different meanings due to different overall story content; the first-to-last sentence similarity metric thus reflects the global semantic structure of a story, despite local textual similarity.

Lexical Predictability.

We utilized a pre-trained language model, GPT-2 Large (774M parameters; Radford et al., 2019), to generate token probabilities, which were then used to calculate surprisal and entropy for each token for each story. For both surprisal and entropy, we computed the mean to capture the overall story predictability, as well as standard deviation to capture how uniform or dynamic information is distributed. Surprisal quantifies how unexpected a specific token is in each context, defined as the negative log-probability of a token given its preceding context (Hale, 2001; Eq. S1). Entropy, on the other hand, quantifies the level of uncertainty about a particular word position given prior context. Specifically, entropy is defined as the expected surprisal over all tokens in the model's vocabulary and is associated with longer reading time (Van Schijndel & Linzen, 2018; Eq. S4). To measure surprisal and entropy over a longer sequence of strings (i.e., narrative)-thus capturing longer-timescale structure-we computed the mean and standard deviation of the surprisal (Eq. S2-3) and entropy for all tokens in the string (Eq. S5-6).

Lexical Composition. This category captures linguistic-emotional expressiveness and the improvisational demands of a story. It includes the number of lexical categories, calculated using Empath (Fast et al., 2016), which classifies words into over 200 pre-validated semantic categories. We also calculated lexical diversity using the type-token ratio (number of unique tokens divided by the total number of tokens; Richards, 1987), and emotionality using the VADER sentiment lexicon (Hutto & Gilbert, 2014), with absolute values of normalized, weighted compound sentiment scores ranging from 0 (least intense) to 1 (most intense). The number of random story elements (e.g., "a pet snake"; "a locked box") in the given prompt was also included to capture the degree of improvisational constraint of the story.

Language Productivity.

Individual metrics in this feature category measure the mere quantity of text, including total word count, sentence count, mean length of utterance (MLU), and the Flesch Readability Score (a score based on sentence length and word syllable complexity, ranging from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating greater ease of reading). These metrics serve as coarse indicators of baseline verbal fluency, syntactic complexity, and linguistic clarity. Metrics that significantly predict human ratings in this category will be used as control variables when evaluating metrics from the other three categories.

Statistical Analysis

We first ran linear mixed-effects models to see whether experts and novices differ in their story ratings, using lme4 (Bates et al., 2015) and lmerTest (Kuznetsova et al., 2017) packages in R. Models included by-story and by-rater random intercepts to account for item-level and subject-level baseline differences. Next, to examine the multidimensional structure of the rating space, we conducted Principal Component Analysis (PCA) using the FactoMineR (Lê et al., 2008) package in R. We also used linear mixed-effects models with the same random structure to examine group differences in the relationships among rating dimensions and links between rating dimensions and linguistic features. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995) was applied to correct for multiple testing each time we examined a main effect (i.e., whether a linguistic feature in the semantic similarity, lexical predictability, or lexical composition categories significantly predicted human ratings). Moderation analyses were then restricted to metrics with significant main effects and used a significance level of α = 0.05. All other statistical tests were also conducted at α = 0.05.

To account for potential practice effects arising from experts rating more stories across multiple sessions than novices, we conducted supplementary analyses (Table S8), which indicated that such effects are unlikely to explain the reported expertise differences. We include a detailed description of the analyses and findings under "Control Analysis" below.

Anonymized raw and processed datasets, as well as R and Python scripts for data preprocessing, wrangling, analysis, and figure generation, are publicly available on OSF: https://osf.io/qzsy3/?view_only=7c75e8804ebc40c78e19cfb4c282eb5b.

Results

Minimal influence of expertise on the overall structure of the story rating space

First, we tested whether experts' and novices' mean ratings differ significantly along five narrative dimensions (creativity, imagination, novelty, complexity, cohesiveness). We ran a linear mixed-effects model to examine whether ratings differed by rater group across the five dimensions, including rater group, dimension, and their interaction as fixed effects, with random intercepts for rater and story. We found no significant main effect of rater group on overall ratings across dimensions (β = -0.12, SE = 0.15, p = 0.424) (Figure 1A). There was a significant interaction between rater group and dimension, and post-hoc simple effects comparisons showed that this was driven by complexity, with experts giving higher complexity ratings than novices (β = -0.40, SE = 0.16, p = 0.010). In contrast, the two groups' ratings did not differ significantly for creativity (β = -0.05, SE = 0.16, p = 0.732), imagination (β = -0.07, SE = 0.16, p = 0.673), novelty (β = -0.09, SE = 0.16, p = 0.582), or cohesiveness (β = 0.12, SE = 0.16, p = 0.423) (All five post-hoc tests above were Bonferroni corrected).

Second, to understand the overall structure of the story rating space, we performed Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on ratings from each group. We identified two optimal principal components in the rating space for both experts and novices by visually inspecting the scree plot using the "elbow" method (Figure S1A -B; Cattell, 1966; Sen & Cohen, 2025).

Analysis of the contributions of each rating dimension to the principal components revealed that, for both groups, the first component reflected a strongly overlapping concept of creativity, novelty, imagination, and complexity, while the other one substantially reflected cohesiveness (Figure 1B). This pattern is consistent with Patel et al. (2025), in which they found creativity and coherence to reflect distinct dimensions of spontaneous speech.

Expertise increases the differentiation between narrative dimensions

Although the overall structure of the rating space was quite similar across groups, we wondered whether the more fine-grained relationships between these five rating dimensions of narrative quality might still differ. To statistically test for potential differences between the pattern of correlation between dimensions, we used linear mixed-effect models predicting each story dimension with another story dimension, rater group, and their interaction term, with by-rater and by-story random intercepts (e.g., Figure 1C). We found that although creativity, imagination, and novelty were significantly correlated in both experts and novices (Figure 1D; see Table S1 for full results), there was a significant interaction between these associations and rater group, indicating that experts had weaker associations between rating dimensions.

Specifically, this interaction with rater group was significant for the association between creativity and novelty (interaction: β = -0.17, SE = 0.03, p < 0.001; Figure 1C), creativity and imagination (β = -0.19, SE = 0.02, p < 0.001), novelty and imagination (β = -0.13, SE = 0.03, p < 0.001), and complexity and novelty (β = -0.09, SE = 0.03, p = 0.008). Additionally, we ruled out the possibility that experts' weaker associations were simply due to less consistent ratings than novices. We compared the internal consistency of ratings for experts and novices using Cronbach's alpha, with shuffled ratings serving as a baseline for comparison. Both experts' and novices' ratings were more internally consistent than shuffled ratings, while their internal reliability did not significantly differ from each other. Thus, the weaker associations among experts were unlikely to reflect lower rating consistency (see Table S2 and Figure S2). Overall, these results indicate that experts have more distinct representations of several of these story dimensions, suggesting a more nuanced rating space overall, compared to novices. all 108 stories. Coordinates of arrow point indicate the correlations between each original story dimension and the first two principal components. Story dimensions that are grouped together and point in the same direction of the plot are positively correlated. The Contribution of Diverse Linguistic Features to Human Ratings

Analytical Approach

The results above suggest that, while experts and novices rate improvised stories similarly overall, they diverge in terms of more fine-grained associations between individual story dimensions. Next, we tested the hypothesis that experts' and novices' ratings may be driven by different linguistic features of stories. We included four categories of metrics: language productivity (overall quantity of content in a story, which we primarily used as a control), semantic similarity, lexical predictability (how expected or surprising a story is), and lexical composition (e.g., the diversity and emotionality of words). Since PCA revealed two distinct, latent components of ratings, we decided to run regression models on two individual story dimensions which were highly representative of each component (i.e., cohesiveness and creativity, the latter of which was highly correlated with novelty, imagination, and complexity; Figures 1B & 1D).

Linear mixed-effect models with by-story and by-rater random intercepts were run to assess which linguistic metrics predicted ratings of creativity and cohesiveness and whether these associations differ across experts and novices. First, we report results from individual models that test one linguistic metric at a time (and the interaction between this metric-rating link and rater group), applying the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (α = 0.05) to account for the false discovery rate due to the large number of models tested. Next, we report the full model with all relevant metrics predicting story ratings to assess their relative contribution to human ratings and qualitatively compare the contributions of experts and novices. Results of main effects and interaction effects for all metrics are reported in Tables S5-S7. All metrics were standardized by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation.

Language Productivity

The language productivity feature has metrics that describe story length (word count, sentence count), utterance complexity (mean length utterance (MLU)) and text difficulty (readability). Table S3 summarizes models where individual metrics predicted each rating dimension. As predicted, stories that had higher word and sentence counts were rated as more creative (β = 0.10, SE = 0.04, p = 0.006; β = 0.08, SE = 0.04, p = 0.039, respectively) but not more cohesive (β = 0.05, SE = 0.03, p = 0.184; β = -0.03, SE = 0.03, p = 0.422, respectively).

On the other hand, stories with longer MLU were rated as more cohesive but not more creative (β = 0.08, SE = 0.03, p = 0.016; β = 0.002, SE = 0.04, p = 0.942, respectively). This pattern of results converges with our PCA findings, such that creativity and cohesiveness are two related but conceptually distinct aspects of overall story quality, driven by different text characteristics.

Readability was not associated with any of the story dimensions, possibly due to a ceiling effect such that all stories are easily readable (see Table S3). We included significant metrics (word count, sentence count, MLU) in the rest of the regression models as controls, in order to see which of the other linguistic metrics predicted ratings beyond the amount of language output.

Semantic Similarity

These metrics describe how similar two linguistic items (e.g., words, sentences) are in meaning. Figure 2A illustrates the process of computing sentence-level semantic similarity metrics using Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020). Figure 2B depicts the only semantic similarity metric, first-to-last sentence similarity, that significantly predicted creativity and cohesiveness ratings. Metrics that capture semantic similarity across all word/sentence pairs and adjacent sentence pairs were not significant predictors (see Table S6 for the statistics of all semantic similarity metrics we analyzed). Contrary to our predictions, the first-to-last sentence similarity metric positively predicted both creativity and cohesiveness (main effect, β = 0.39, SE = 0.09, p(corrected) < 0.001; β = 0.23, SE = 0.08, p(corrected) = 0.040, respectively). Experts showed a weaker effect of the first-to-last sentence similarity metric on creativity (Figure 2B, middle; interaction effect, β = -0.10, SE = 0.03, p = 0.002). This result suggests that novice ratings were more driven by linguistic features than expert ratings. the key semantic similarity metrics (right). Lexical Predictability

Metrics in this feature category include word surprisal and word entropy, both of which capture important aspects of information complexity and language processing. Contrary to our prediction, creativity ratings were not predicted by surprisal mean or standard deviation (surprisal mean: main effect, β = 0.06, SE = 0.04, p(corrected) = 0.493; surprisal SD: main effect, β = 0.06, SE = 0.04, p(corrected) = 0.363; Figure 3A, middle top and bottom, respectively). For cohesiveness, on the contrary, as expected, higher ratings were predicted by lower surprisal mean and standard deviation (surprisal mean: main effect, β = -0.10, SE = 0.03, p(corrected) = 0.029; surprisal SD: main effect, β = -0.09, SE = 0.03, p(corrected) = 0.048) and lower entropy mean (main effect, β = -0.09, SE = 0.03, p(corrected) = 0.045). Rater group also significantly moderated the relationship between these metrics and cohesiveness ratings, such that experts showed weaker associations than novices (surprisal mean: interaction effect, β = 0.07, SE = 0.03, p = 0.024, Figure 3A, top right; surprisal SD: interaction effect, β = 0.07, SE = 0.03, p = 0.022, Figure 3A, bottom right; entropy mean: interaction effect, β = 0.08, SE = 0.03, p = 0.016, Figure 3B, top right). In line with the findings above for semantic similarity, these results provide evidence that experts' ratings were less driven by lexical predictability metrics as well. Lexical composition

This category captures other characteristics relating to the semantic content, emotional expressiveness, and improvisational demands of the story, including sentiment, lexical diversity, lexical categories, and the number of prompt elements that were used in the story (see Tables S5-S7 for the full set of model statistics across all metrics). Figure 4 summarizes the interaction results for the significant lexical composition metric. As predicted, there was a significant main effect of lexical diversity on creativity (i.e., both groups rated stories that contain more distinct words as more creative) (β = 0.15, SE = 0.04, p(corrected) = 0.019). Additionally, the number of random elements provided in the story prompt (1-3) negatively predicted cohesiveness (i.e., stories based on more elements were rated as less cohesive) (main effect, β = -0.11, SE = 0.04, p(corrected) = 0.044), and once again, this relationship was weaker for experts than for novices (interaction effect, β = 0.10, SE = 0.04, p = 0.011, Figure 4, right). statistics for predicting creativity and cohesiveness separately. Control analysis

Because experts and novices had different survey structures (i.e., each expert completed six sessions, whereas each novice completed one session only), we conducted an additional analysis to see whether the observed expertise effects could be driven by experts completing more sessions and rating more stories, rather than by true expertise differences. We focused on results that showed significant group differences. We directly tested the influence of session by running polynomial mixed-effects regression models to test whether inter-dimension relationships and feature-to-rating relationships changed across expert sessions (modeled as a second-order polynomial with by-story and by-rater random intercepts). No significant linear or quadratic trends were observed across sessions (Table S8), indicating that the reported group differences cannot be explained by differences in task exposure or practice effects between experts and novices.

Full model

Finally, to directly compare the relative impact of different metrics on story ratings, we entered all significant metrics above into the same model (one model for creativity, one for cohesiveness), while controlling for word count, sentence count, and MLU, with by-story and by-rater random intercepts (Figure 5). For creativity, results showed that for both rater groups, the first-to-last sentence similarity metric had the largest effect, followed by lexical diversity. As for cohesiveness, the first-to-last sentence similarity metric was also the strongest predictor for both groups. Additionally, the number of story elements predicted novices' cohesiveness ratings (but not experts'). Moreover, although we were unable to systematically test whether coefficient magnitudes differed significantly between groups due to constraints of model convergence, the overall pattern suggests that magnitude tended to be smaller for experts than for novices. Taken together, these results suggest that first-to-last semantic similarity is an important signature of both creativity and cohesiveness. Lexical diversity was a significant predictor of creativity only, and this pattern was observed in both groups. Stories improvised under greater constraints (i.e., with a larger number of elements) were rated as less cohesive, particularly by novices. Overall, while experts and novices were influenced by similar linguistic features, novices relied more heavily on these features when evaluating both creativity and cohesiveness. predicted creativity or cohesiveness.
