Discussion

Taking a holistic approach that uses several categories of linguistic features to predict human ratings of stories, our study offers important insights into the multidimensional nature of narrative perception in the understudied but highly ecologically relevant domain of improvised storytelling. Overall, experts and novices had largely similar overall rating values across the dimensions tested (Figure 1A), except that experts gave higher ratings for complexity than novices. Additionally, the perceptual rating space of both groups shared a similar two-component structure (reflecting creativity vs. cohesiveness; Figure 1B). However, experts and novices did differ in how their ratings of the five dimensions related to one another. Specifically, all of the pairwise associations among creativity, imagination, and novelty (which were the most correlated among the five overall), were perceived as more separable by experts than novices. This suggests that experts may have developed more precise and distinct representations of individual but related story dimensions, whereas novices treat those dimensions as more interchangeable. In addition, experts' ratings were less strongly driven by underlying linguistic features than novices (Figures 2 3 4). For example, creativity was more strongly predicted by first-to-last sentence similarity in novices than experts, and cohesiveness was more strongly predicted by several lexical predictability metrics and number of elements in novices than in experts as well. We also found that different metrics reflected different aspects of a narrative's perceived quality. Together, our results suggest that measuring fine-grained relationships between different structural dimensions of creative products, as well as ratings of them, opens new possibilities for advancing our understanding of creativity more broadly in increasingly naturalistic contexts and diverse populations.

Our finding that experts and novices did not differ in their mean ratings at the group level is consistent with some relevant prior literature on written stories (Kaufman et al., 2009; Taylor et al., 2021). However, similar mean ratings do not necessarily imply similar patterns of evaluation within individuals. Our analyses of inter-dimension and feature-rating relationships therefore provide a more fine-grained view of within-rater structure and offer insight into theoretically meaningful frameworks of expertise. Particularly, the more nuanced and less feature-driven patterns observed in expert ratings suggest differences in underlying cognitive and perceptual mechanisms that are masked by converging group-level means. In this sense, expertise is expressed not in higher or lower scores, but in how evaluative judgments are internally organized. Specifically, experts' knowledge and experience may shape their perceptual sensitivity and weighting of narrative cues, leading to reduced reliance on the particular features quantified here compared to novices. Underlying these differences are well-established cognitive mechanisms of expertise development. For example, adaptive perceptual learning enables experts to efficiently extract information and discriminate fine-grained, subordinate-level details through repeated experience (Kellman & Garrigan, 2009; Herzmann & Curran, 2011). In addition, enhanced working memory and attentional control in skilled individuals support the integration and retention of multiple information sources, which facilitates more holistic and flexible evaluations (Moore et al., 2008). Domain-relevant knowledge and exposure give rise to the formation of experts' internal schemas, and it guides experts to interpret stimuli at a more abstract level rather than relying on literal, surface features (Chi, 2006; Chi et al., 1981).

Another goal of the study was to better understand the complex space of story dimensions and why experts and novices differ by using metrics from linguistics and deep natural language processing models to examine linguistic and structural features of improvised narratives. This approach highlighted a novel similarity metric-first-to-last sentence similarity-that predicts creativity and was the most predictive metric among all metrics we considered. We came up with this metric because storytellers were instructed to begin and end their stories with fixed sentences given a priori, which was meant to help participants get started with telling stories and to avoid unfocused storytelling. Furthermore, although the beginning and end sentences were highly similar across all stories, their representations in Longformer were dependent on the rest of the story content. Therefore, we reasoned that the difference between the Longformer embeddings for the first and last sentence of an improvised narrative may likely capture a key aspect of the overall story content. Additionally, because token order adds important contextual information in the Longformer model, the contents of the known boundaries of each story would serve as unique anchor points for capturing thematic development of the story -features that may be relevant to specific story qualities and are conceptually distinct from local variation and narrative flow across a story (e.g., sentence-to-sentence or word-to-word similarity). Here, we found that first-to-last sentence similarity was positively associated with creativity and its overlapping dimensions, as well as cohesiveness. This finding is consistent with prior work showing that lower semantic distance (i.e., higher semantic similarity) is related to greater verbal fluency (Reilly et al., 2023; Zemla, 2022). At the same time, this finding contrasts with prior work showing that higher semantic distance (i.e., smaller semantic similarity) between words predicts higher creativity in verbal and divergent thinking tasks (Prabhakaran et al., 2014; Heinen & Johnson, 2018; Beaty & Johnson, 2021; Johnson et al., 2022) and story success (Toubia et al., 2021). Relatedly, story endings with a larger semantic distance from a provided story context are rated as more original (Fan et al., 2023). Conversely, our work shows that it is possible that certain aspects of semantic similarity may indeed be positively correlated with creativity: in the context of narratives, higher semantic similarity between the beginning and the end of an improvised narrative might suggest a more consistent theme over the course of the story, or a more successful weaving of distantly related ideas into a cohesive and convergent narrative.

Nevertheless, future work should validate the robustness of this metric using multiple language models (e.g., directly contrasting contextual and non-contextual models) and cognitive tasks.

Other metrics we considered were more narrowly associated with each story dimension separately. For example, lexical surprisal mean and standard deviation, as well as entropy mean, were negatively associated with cohesiveness, consistent with literature showing that high surprisal and entropy words lead to higher processing effort (Lowder et al., 2018). Lexical diversity predicted perceived creativity exclusively, which is consistent with existing findings showing that creativity is associated with a more sophisticated lexicon (Skalicky et al., 2017; McNamara et al., 2010). On the other hand, number of prompt elements predicted cohesiveness exclusively, suggesting that a story's improvisational demand may drive the perception of overall narrative flow, but does not necessarily add to the creativity and novelty of the story content.

Altogether, the differentiation between creativity vs. cohesiveness we found for the perceptual rating space dovetails their distinct, nuanced structural mechanisms, building on existing findings that cohesion and creativity are distinct features (Zedelius et al., 2019; Patel et al., 2025; McNamara et al., 2010; Fan et al., 2023). Importantly, our analyses extend this work by providing a linguistic feature-based account of this distinction, showing that creativity and cohesiveness are associated with different profiles of linguistic and semantic features.

Next, by entering all linguistic metrics across all feature categories into one comprehensive model (Figure 5), we aimed to directly compare each metric to the others with one unified statistical approach to better understand their relative importance to judgments of creativity and cohesiveness. In the full model, for creativity, our first-to-last sentence similarity metric was the most predictive, followed by lexical diversity. Moreover, the ranking of metrics predicting creativity was broadly similar across experts and novices, suggesting that both groups relied on largely comparable linguistic and semantic cues when evaluating stories. Interestingly, a notable difference was that novices, but not experts, were more influenced by language productivity measures (i.e., word count, sentence count, MLU), suggesting that novices may place greater weight on surface-level indicators of verbal output when forming their evaluations, whereas experts may look beyond these more salient features and attend to less obvious, more nuanced aspects of narrative features. As for cohesiveness, both groups were influenced by first-to-last sentence similarity and word count. Novice ratings were also driven by MLU and number of prompt elements. The presence of these additional metrics, as well as the larger magnitude of association between them for novices, showcases how experts and novices factored these linguistic and structural features into their rating judgments differently. Specifically, we found that experts' ratings were driven less overall by structural features of stories and less influenced by basic text properties than novices' ratings. This suggests that experts may take a more holistic approach to assessing creativity than novices, an interpretation also supported by the perceptual expertise literature in visual processing (e.g., Gauthier et al., 1998; Gauthier & Tarr, 2002; Richler et al., 2011).

Our consideration of a uniquely large number of diverse linguistic features adds significant breadth to the current understanding of the underlying structural mechanisms of story perception. Some of the linguistic features we measured are highly interpretable. For instance, language productivity metrics (e.g., word count) provide a direct measure of text volume. Their strong positive association with creativity and cohesiveness is consistent with previous findings (e.g., Forthmann et al., 2018). Metrics capturing lexical predictability, linguistic complexity, and task-related language production constraints were also found to be relevant to narrative quality.

By leveraging distributional approximations of semantic relationships, our embedding-based metrics (Figure 3) are also powerful in capturing subtle and complex patterns in language. These additional metrics offer valuable insights into how creative and cohesive storytelling may be reflected in linguistic patterns, and they open up computational avenues for further exploring the mechanisms of narrative perception. Importantly, many of these metrics have not been studied together, and there were few studies that examined these metrics in long improvised spoken stories. This study, therefore, by using a more descriptive and associative lens, lays the groundwork for future experimental manipulations to further understand the underlying mechanisms of story perception. Specifically, generative AI offers the possibility of systematically manipulating some of these metrics (e.g., surprisal) within the same stories, to directly test their impact (on both novices and experts) in a more controlled way. In general, we encourage cautious interpretation of our metric-related findings, but we believe our novel exploratory approach was necessary to help uncover broad patterns in the links between structural features and creativity, and to generate hypotheses for more targeted investigations in the future.

Our findings reveal meaningful differences between experts' and novices' judgments of improvised spoken narratives, but there are further aspects of these expertise effects to explore. It is also possible that other narrative features not captured in the current analyses (e.g., common literary devices, aspects of character and plot development (D 'Souza, 2021), integration of different prompt elements, etc.) may play a larger role in driving experts' ratings compared to novices', and our results highlight the need to further investigate which specific aspects of storytelling are most salient to creative writing experts. Although we were limited in our ability to recruit a large sample of highly trained storytelling experts, future work could better isolate different kinds of expertise in creative storytelling (e.g., creative writing graduates vs. filmmakers vs. improvisational performers) and recruit specific cohorts targeting these sub-cohorts. In addition to a binary grouping of experts and novices, having a continuous view of expertise (e.g., from minimally experienced, to quasi-expert, to expert) or a multi-dimensional characterization of expertise (e.g., amount of casual exposure vs. formal training) may reveal more nuanced expertise effects on narrative perception (Kaufman & Baer, 2012; Farrington-Darby & Wilson, 2006). Further investigation of these factors may also offer deeper insights into how the mechanisms underlying narrative perception are influenced by possessing a high level of explicit knowledge, skills, and/or years of experience in a particular domain.

Importantly, our analyses accounted for both speaker-level and item-level variability.

However, there are some interesting questions relating to these factors for future work to explore.

As noted in recent studies (Anderson et al., 2023; Pombo et al., 2024), certain works of art may elicit higher consensus among raters, while others may be more ambiguous or polarizing, leading to greater disagreement. In the domain of storytelling, it is still unclear what features might drive this polarization. Likewise, some storytellers (even within the general population sampled in our Prolific pool) may be consistently more creative than others, and follow-up work could search for common narrative strategies or structural patterns that distinguish or cluster these storytellers based on their baseline or default level of creativity.

Overall, our findings provide new and compelling evidence for subtle but meaningful differences in how experts and novices assess various qualities of improvised spoken narratives.

Both experts and novices shared a similar principal component structure in their rating space, represented by creativity and cohesiveness. Experts showed more differentiation between a few story dimensions, and their ratings relied less strongly overall on linguistic and structural features of narratives, compared to novices. We also introduced a new metric-first-to-last sentence similarity-which outperformed other linguistic features in predicting both creativity and cohesiveness. The use of improvised oral storytelling further distinguishes our work, making our findings informative as to how naturalistic, everyday narratives may be perceived. Improvised storytelling is a pervasive and ecologically valid form of everyday communication, underlying activities such as conversation and social interaction, explanation and teaching, caregiving and play, comedy, and more. This study provides a valuable window into creative cognition under naturalistic constraints, complementing prior work that has largely focused on shorter and more polished creative written works. Our findings indicate that expertise shapes the internal organization of story dimensions and the perceptual weighting of linguistic features, even when experts and novices converge in their overall ratings. This distinction highlights the importance of examining underlying mechanisms beyond surface-level agreement, with implications for models of expertise, rater training, and the interpretation of creative evaluation data. Together, by combining rich human ratings, computational models, and quantitative metrics, we have brought a new understanding of the multidimensional space of human story perception, providing a scalable framework for future research on the mechanisms underlying judgments of creative works.

Cronbach's alpha between novice, expert, and shuffled ratings

We generated a randomly shuffled dataset based on the expert ratings, and then conducted a linear regression model with rater group predicting Cronbach's alphas to test whether ratings from novices, experts, and randomly shuffled data differed in internal consistency. Results showed no significant difference in internal consistency between novices and experts, but both groups were significantly more consistent than the shuffled ratings (see Table for model statistics; expert alpha M = 0.78, SD = 0.08; novice alpha M = 0.67, SD = 0.46; shuffled ratings alpha M = 0.02, SD = 0.11). These findings indicate that although experts showed lower associations between dimensions, their ratings were highly consistent and comparable to those of novices. This supports the idea that experts' rating patterns reflect a systematic perspective, rather than random variability.

Analyses Controlling for Potential Practice Effects

To examine whether the observed expertise effects could be explained by experts having more survey sessions and rating more stories, rather than by true expertise differences, we conducted an additional analysis. We focused specifically on results that showed significant group differences and directly tested the effect of session order within expert ratings. Polynomial mixed-effects regression models were used to examine whether inter-dimensional relationships and feature-rating associations differed systematically across expert sessions (i.e., linearly or nonlinearly). The expert session variable was treated as a discrete numeric predictor ranging from 1 to 6, with larger values indicating later sessions. It was modeled as a second-order polynomial, and by-story and by-rater random intercepts were included. If there are significant changes across sessions, this would suggest that the original effects may reflect differences in task exposure or rating experience during the study rather than expertise in storytelling.

Table S8 reports the statistics of the polynomial mixed-effects regression models. No significant linear or quadratic trends were found across expert sessions. Therefore, the group differences observed in the original analyses are unlikely to be explained by differences in the survey structures between experts and novices.
